questiontext.text:
UniCV prototype for "predict the result" questions in Python. The student works out, without running the code, the value (and optionally the type) of some expressions and the output of some short programs. The values in the code can be random, so that each attempt is different. The teacher never writes the correct answers: the grader computes them by running the code with Python, for the values of each attempt.

How to write a question

  1. Write the items in the Global extra field, in sections (see the example below):
    • ## context: code run before every item and shown to the student under "Consider:" (e.g. a list or a text used by the expressions).
    • ## expressions: one expression per line; the student gives its value and type.
    • ## values: one expression per line; the student gives only its value.
    • ## output: the following lines are a program; the student writes what it prints. If the program reads data, give it in the header, separated by semicolons: ## output input: 4; 7.
    Without any section header, every line is an expression with value and type. Lines starting with # in the expression sections are ignored.
  2. For random values: in Template params write, for example, {"a": {{ random(10, 30) }}, "b": {{ random(2, 6) }}, "city": "{{ random(["Praia", "Mindelo", "Assomada"]) }}"}, set the language of the template parameters to twig, tick Twig all, and write {{ a }}, {{ b }}, {{ city }} in Global extra (and in the question text if needed). Each attempt gets its own values; the same student keeps them during the attempt. random(10, 30) gives an integer from 10 to 30 and random([...]) one element of the list.
  3. Leave the Answer field as the interface fills it (there is nothing to write) and keep Validate on save ticked: saving checks that every item runs (an item that takes too long, or a context that fails, is reported).
  4. To see the correct answers for some values, preview the question, click Fill in correct responses and then Check: the feedback shows a table with all the answers.

Example of Global extra (with the template parameters above):

## context
numbers = [{{ a }}, {{ b }}, 1, 9]
city = "{{ city }}"
## expressions
{{ a }} // {{ b }} + {{ a }} % {{ b }}
city[::-1]
numbers[1:3]
"7" + {{ b }}
## values
len(city) * 2
## output input: {{ b }}
num = int(input("num? "))
for k in range(num):
    if k % 2 == 0:
        print(k)

What the student gets

  • The context code, a table of expressions with a box for the value and a list for the type (int, float, str, bool, list, tuple, dict, set, NoneType, range or Error), and for each program its code with line numbers, the input typed on the keyboard and a box for the output.
  • A counter of the answers given, a Help panel and a Start again button (with confirmation).
  • After Check, each answer is marked in green or red, and a table summarises the results.

How answers are compared

  • Values are read as Python literals and must have the right type: 4 is not 4.0, and 1 is not True. Floats are compared with a tiny tolerance, so 3.50 is accepted for 3.5. Spaces do not matter in lists, tuples and dictionaries.
  • Texts can be written with quotes ('abab', as Python shows them) or without them (abab), unless requirequotes is true.
  • If an expression raises an error, the correct answer is the type Error and, as the value, the name of the error (e.g. TypeError).
  • The output of a program is compared line by line; spaces at the end of lines and empty lines at the end are ignored. If the program reads data, what is typed also appears in the output (e.g. num? 4), as on a screen. If the program stops with an error, the name of the error is its last line.
  • The mark is the fraction of correct answers (each value and each type counts as one answer), unless All-or-nothing grading is ticked.

Limitations

  • Expressions must fit on one line; longer code goes in ## context or in an ## output program.
  • In Global extra, Twig is used only to insert values ({{ a }}); the random values are chosen in Template params.
  • Values that are not literals (e.g. objects) are compared with how Python shows them (their repr).
  • Moodle's emoticon filter turns some short texts in brackets, such as the letters n, y or i between round brackets, into icons in the question text and in the code shown to the student. Avoid them (e.g. write range(num)) or turn off the emoticon filter for the course.

Template parameters (all optional, besides the random values)

  • showcorrect (default false): if true, the correct answer is shown for each wrong answer after Check (useful for practice, not for tests).
  • requirequotes (default false): if true, texts must be written with quotes, as Python shows them.
  • echostandardinput (default true): if false, the values read by input() do not appear in the output.
  • timeout (default 2): time limit in seconds for each item.
  • maxoutputlength (default 5000): longer outputs are cut.

Example: {"a": {{ random(10, 30) }}, "b": {{ random(2, 6) }}, "showcorrect": true}
